extraction.name: NWPU-RESISC45
extraction.description: A freely and publicly available benchmark for remote sensing image scene classification containing 31,500 RGB images across 45 scene classes, with 700 images per class and an image size of 256×256 pixels. Images cover more than 100 countries and regions worldwide. The dataset emphasizes rich image variations, high within-class diversity, and high between-class similarity.
extraction.creator: Northwestern Polytechnical University (NWPU)
extraction.citeAs: Gong Cheng, Junwei Han, and Xiaoqiang Lu. Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification: Benchmark and State of the Art. Accepted by Proceedings of the IEEE.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Experts in remote sensing image interpretation extracted images from Google Earth. The 31,500 images cover more than 100 countries and regions, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies. Images were carefully selected under different weather, season, illumination, imaging, and scale conditions. To select scene categories, the authors investigated existing datasets to identify 30 widely used categories, then searched Web of Science and Google Scholar using the keywords OBIA, GEOBIA, land cover classification, land use classification, geographic image retrieval, and geospatial object detection to select 15 additional meaningful classes.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Google Earth (Google Inc.), which maps the Earth by superimposing satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system information onto a 3D globe. Spatial resolution ranges from approximately 30 m to 0.2 m per pixel for most classes; island, lake, mountain, and snowberg images have lower spatial resolutions.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For benchmarking, the dataset was randomly split using two training-test ratios: 10%-90%, corresponding to 70 training and 630 testing images per class, and 20%-80%, corresponding to 140 training and 560 testing images per class. Experiments were repeated ten times for each ratio. CNN fine-tuning was performed without data augmentation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were extracted from Google Earth, and the resulting dataset consists of 256×256-pixel images in RGB color space.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Images are divided into 45 scene classes, with 700 images in each class. The class vocabulary was constructed by selecting 30 widely used categories from existing datasets and 15 additional meaningful categories through literature searches. Scene classes encompass land use and land cover, man-made objects, and natural landscape objects. The paper states that experts in remote sensing image interpretation extracted the images but does not detail the label-assignment procedure.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to benefit the remote sensing research community by enabling the development and evaluation of new data-driven algorithms at a larger scale and supporting progress in remote sensing image scene classification.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has high within-class diversity and between-class similarity, including fine-grained classes with substantial semantic overlap. Benchmark results show notable confusion between church and palace and between dense residential and medium residential because of similar global structures or spatial layouts. The concluding discussion identifies shortcomings of relying only on overhead remote sensing imagery: ground photographs can provide additional detail and vertical characteristics, and social media and location-based resources can supply complementary information.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Development, training, testing, fine-tuning, and benchmarking of remote sensing image scene classification algorithms. The paper evaluates handcrafted features, unsupervised feature-learning methods, pretrained CNN features, and fine-tuned CNN features. Its benchmark uses random 10%-90% and 20%-80% training-test splits, repeats experiments ten times per split ratio, and reports overall accuracy, standard deviation, and confusion matrices.
